newsitem.title: KENYA: Coffee prices firm in Kenya, steady in Uganda.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices firm in Kenya, steady in Uganda.

text.p: Coffee prices were firm at Kenyan export auctions due to declining quantities but held steady in leading exporter Uganda.
Traders said on Wednesday Kenyan coffee fetched large premiums for better qualities at Tuesday's auction and prices for lower qualities were reasonable.
"(Grade) AB was $26 over New York (December) while AA was $30 over," one senior trader said.

The trader said lack of coffee could be one reason why prices were rising, adding that it was known on the market that the Coffee Board of Kenya had problems getting a catalogue of what it had placed on offer published in advance.

"The board has already sold much this year but coffee is still coming in slowly. There is a worry there. People are in (the market) for covering for their requirements a little earlier just in case we run dry," the trader added.

Another trader said regional sanctions imposed on the central African state of Burundi meant Burundian coffees did not come into the market. That had resulted in some buyers having to take more Kenyan coffee as a replacement.
"The problem is that at around now, only Kenya, Burundi and Tanzania can claim to have fresh coffees," the trader said.
Regional sanctions were imposed after the July 25 coup by Burundi's mainly Tutsi army.
An official at a top Kenyan coffee house said the coffee board planned to offer only 21,000 60-kg bags of coffee for sale next week compared to just 33,060 bags sold on Tuesday.

"The week after that we do not know whether we will have enough. If the trend goes like that, whatever is available will be very expensibe," the official said. "November, we may have no auctions and December, as usual, will have very little coffee."
But the official said quality was good "Current crop quality is good for those who don't like strong coffee; on average it is considered good for the time of the year."
Prices have risen at the Nairobi auction for the last two weeks, even when the New York market was seen declining.

An official from the Uganda Coffee Trade Federation said the main season in the central parts of Buganda and Busoga had just started. "I have received reports of people bringing in very dry coffee as compared to last season," he said.
He added farmers had kept their coffee hoping that prices would go up but were now selling to meet pressing obligations.
"The rain is on but the crop is dry. We think we will have a good crop," the official said. "The moisture content is just below the statutory allowed and we are looking good."
The official said that on average the coffee was around $230 below London, slightly lower than in recent months.
"The situation (versus London) is very bearish," he said.
But he added that Ugandan shilling depreciations meant returns to growers remained "reasonably healthy".
Statistics on September coffee auctions in the northern Tanzanian coffee town of Moshi were not immediately available and officials declined to give forecasts.

But Switzerland-based Edm Schluter & Co Ltd said of the Tanzanian market "There has been good demand for the new crop coffes from the market, both from the Far East and Europe." --Nairobi Newsroom ++254-2 330-261.
